Maybe you've had a question you were afraid to say out loud, a prayer that felt like it hit the ceiling, or a moment in church when everyone else seemed sure and you weren't.

This session says something that may surprise you: doubt is not the opposite of faith. In Mark 9, a desperate father says to Jesus, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24), and Jesus helps him. In John 20, the disciple Thomas says he won't believe Jesus rose from the dead unless he sees it for himself. Jesus doesn't throw him out. He comes back, shows Thomas his wounds, and Thomas says, “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). Even on the day Jesus gave his followers their mission, Matthew says they worshiped him, “but some doubted” (Matthew 28:17).

Owning your faith doesn't mean starting from scratch, and it doesn't mean pretending. The second letter to Timothy, written in Paul's name to a young leader, remembers a faith that “first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice” and now lives in Timothy too (2 Timothy 1:5). Faith becomes yours when you bring your real questions to Jesus and keep following him while you ask them. You're allowed to ask. He isn't afraid of your questions.

keyScripture.why: Thomas refuses to believe the resurrection on anyone else's word and asks to see for himself, and Jesus answers not by shaming him but by coming back and showing him his wounds, which shows that honest doubt brought to Jesus can end in one of the fullest confessions in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28).

discussion.q: Without naming anyone, what questions about God or faith do people your age carry but rarely say out loud in church?
discussion.behind: Keep it general and welcome everything. You may hear: Is any of this real? Why does God allow suffering? Why do Christians act like hypocrites? Is Christianity the only way? What about science? Write the questions down and don't answer them yet. Thank the room. The point is to show that questions can be spoken here without anyone panicking. If one question is clearly heavy for a particular student, offer to talk afterward, somewhere others can see you.

discussion.q: Thomas said he'd never believe unless he saw the nail marks for himself (John 20:25). When Jesus came back, what did he do, and what didn't he do?
discussion.behind: Jesus came back eight days later, spoke peace, and offered Thomas exactly the evidence he had asked for (John 20:26-27). He didn't shame him or throw him out of the group. He did tell him to stop doubting and believe, so don't let the room conclude that doubt is a place to live forever. Jesus meets doubt in order to lead it somewhere, to the confession “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). Notice too that Thomas was with the disciples the second time. He didn't walk away while he doubted.

discussion.q: The father in Mark 9 said, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Can belief and unbelief live in the same person at the same time?
discussion.behind: Yes, and that's the point. Os Guinness describes doubt as being in two minds, caught between faith and unbelief, which is different from having decided against God. The father's prayer is honest, and Jesus answers it by healing his son (Mark 9:25-27). Help students see that they can pray the father's prayer. Leaders who have prayed it themselves can say so; it helps students to hear that adults have honest prayers too.

discussion.q: Timothy's faith first lived in his grandmother and his mother, and the letter tells him to continue in what he learned, “since you know from whom you have learned them” (2 Timothy 3:14). Why do the people who hand us faith matter, and what makes a faith become your own?
discussion.behind: Protect both sides. Faith handed down is a gift, not a trap; Timothy had known the Scriptures from infancy (2 Timothy 3:15), and the people who taught him were part of why he could trust what he learned. But the letter says that faith now lives “in you as well” (2 Timothy 1:5). Owning faith doesn't mean rejecting what you were given. It means examining it, the way the Bereans “examined the Scriptures every day” (Acts 17:11), and choosing to trust Christ yourself. Be careful with students whose parents don't share the faith or whose home is hard; for them, the people who hand them faith may be a grandparent, a coach, or this church.

discussion.q: When many followers left Jesus, Peter said, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68). What could it look like to keep following Jesus while you still have questions?
discussion.behind: Close on following, not on certainty. Peter didn't understand everything Jesus had just said, and many who heard it walked away. But he knew where life was. Owning faith often looks like that: honest questions, and a decision to stay close to Jesus while you look for answers. Invite students to think of one question they'd like to keep exploring and an adult they could explore it with, but don't ask anyone to share their answer.

objections.objection: Questioning is just rebellion. The letter of James compares the one who doubts to a wave tossed by the wind and tells him not to expect anything from God. Good Christian kids don't doubt; they believe what they're taught.
objections.response: Grant what's right here. Humility matters, honoring your parents matters (Exodus 20:12), and not every question is honest; some are excuses to do what we already wanted. The letter of James does warn against doubting. But read it in context. It's about asking God for wisdom while being “double-minded” (James 1:8), trying to keep one foot with God and one foot out, not about honest questions brought to God. The same Bible that holds that warning also holds Thomas, whom Jesus came back for, and the father who prayed “help my unbelief” (Mark 9:24), whom Jesus helped, and the command to “have mercy on those who doubt” (Jude 1:22). The boy Jesus himself, at twelve, sat in the temple “listening to them and asking them questions” (Luke 2:46). A question honestly brought to God is a form of faith.

objections.objection: To have my own faith, I have to throw out everything my parents taught me and figure it out from scratch. Otherwise it's just their faith, or just my culture.
objections.response: There's real truth in this. Nobody can believe for you, and a faith only borrowed to keep the peace at home isn't the same as trusting Christ yourself. Some of what gets passed down as Christianity is thin, too, like the moralistic therapeutic deism described in this session's teaching, and that deserves to be questioned. But nobody figures anything out from scratch. Everyone starts with something they were handed, and the person who throws out their parents' faith often just picks up the faith of their feed instead. Owning your faith means examining what you were given honestly, keeping what is true, and coming to trust Jesus for yourself. Timothy's faith first lived in his grandmother and his mother, and it became his own (2 Timothy 1:5). That's what it looks like to inherit a faith rather than rent one.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: If people your age could ask God one question and get a straight answer, what do you think they'd ask? Answer for people in general.
sessions.practice: This week, write down one honest question you have about God or faith, the real one. Then do three things with it. First, pray it the way the father in Mark 9 did: I do believe; help my unbelief. Second, read John 20 slowly, all the way through, and notice how Jesus treats people who aren't sure. Third, bring your question to an adult you trust, a parent, a grandparent, a pastor, or a youth leader, and ask what they think. You don't need an answer by the end of the week. You only need to stop carrying the question alone.
sessions.closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, you came back for Thomas. You didn't leave him outside with his questions, and you didn't leave the father in Mark 9 alone with his unbelief. Some of us are sure tonight, some of us aren't, and some of us have been pretending. Thank you that we don't have to pretend with you. Forgive us, the adults, for the times we've handed young people a faith too thin to survive their questions, and for hiding our own doubts instead of bringing them to you. Give every student here a faith that is truly theirs, received with gratitude from the people who loved them and tested in the light of your word. We do believe. Help our unbelief. Amen.
reflection: What do I actually believe about Jesus right now, apart from what I'm expected to say?
What question have I been afraid to ask, and who could I ask it with?
What have the people who love me handed me about faith that I want to keep, and why?
sessions.teaching:
Start with the situation many students in the room are in, whether or not they'll say so. They grew up around church. They know the songs and the stories and the right answers. And somewhere along the way, maybe this year, a question arrived that they didn't know what to do with. Is any of this real? Why doesn't God answer? Why do Christians act the way they do? Do I believe this, or have I just been around it my whole life? For many students the question is less frightening than what might happen if they asked it out loud: the worried face, the quick verse, the sense that they've let someone down. So they keep quiet, and the question grows in the dark.

There are two common answers. The first says that questioning is rebellion: good Christian kids believe what they're taught, and doubt is sin. It's right that humility matters, that honoring your parents matters, and that some questions are really excuses. The second says that to have a faith of your own you have to throw out everything you were taught and start from scratch, because anything inherited is just your parents' faith or your culture. It's right that nobody can believe for you and that some of what gets passed down as Christianity is thin. But both answers leave out the same person. The first treats questions as a threat to Jesus, and the second assumes he isn't really there to be asked.

We adults need to own our part. In 2005 the sociologist Christian Smith and his colleague Melinda Lundquist Denton published Soul Searching, a national study of American teenagers' religious lives. They found that many teenagers, including many who went to church, held a quiet working creed they called moralistic therapeutic deism: God exists, wants people to be good and nice, helps when you need him, and the point of life is to be happy and feel good about yourself. Five years later Kenda Creasy Dean argued in Almost Christian that teenagers learned that creed mostly from us, from the adults and churches around them. If you were handed a faith that's mostly about being nice and feeling okay, of course it can't hold up under real questions. It was never the faith of the Bible. The faith of the Bible has a cross and an empty tomb at its center, and it was built to survive questions.

So look at how Jesus treats people who aren't sure. In Mark 9 a father brings his son, who has suffered since childhood, after Jesus' disciples have failed to help. The father asks Jesus to help them if he can. Jesus answers, “All things are possible to him who believes!” and the father cries out, “I do believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:23-24). That's belief and unbelief in the same breath, and Jesus doesn't send him away to sort it out first. He heals the boy. In John 20, Thomas wasn't there when the risen Jesus first appeared to the disciples, and he refused to believe on anyone else's word. “Unless I see the nail marks in His hands,” he said, he would never believe (John 20:25). Eight days later Jesus came back, stood among them, and offered Thomas exactly what he'd asked for, and Thomas's doubt ended in one of the clearest confessions of who Jesus is anywhere in the Gospels: “My Lord and my God!” (John 20:28). And when Jesus gathered his followers on a mountain to give them their mission, Matthew says, “they worshiped Him, but some doubted” (Matthew 28:17). Jesus gave the mission to all of them. Os Guinness describes doubt as being in two minds, caught between faith and unbelief. Unbelief has decided against God. Doubt is a question you can still bring to him.

So what does it mean to own your faith? Look at Timothy. The second letter to Timothy, written in Paul's name to a young church leader, remembers his “sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice,” and says that it now lives “in you as well” (2 Timothy 1:5). Later the letter tells him to “continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them. From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures” (2 Timothy 3:14-15). The people mattered. Timothy could trust what he'd been taught partly because he knew who had taught him and how they had lived. But the faith became his own. Owning faith isn't starting over. It's examining what you were handed, the way the Bereans “examined the Scriptures every day to see if these teachings were true” (Acts 17:11), and then choosing to trust Christ yourself. Some of you were handed faith by your parents. Some of you weren't, and your faith came through a grandparent, a coach, a friend, or this church. Either way the question is the same: will you bring your real questions to Jesus and keep following him while you ask them?

When many of Jesus' followers walked away because his teaching was hard, he asked the Twelve if they wanted to leave too. Peter didn't claim to understand everything. He said, “Lord, to whom would we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68). That's what an owned faith often sounds like: not the absence of questions, but the decision to bring them to the one who has the words of life. If you're not a Christian and you came tonight anyway, you're welcome here, and nobody wants you to pretend. Thomas's question was a question about evidence, whether Jesus really rose, and that's a question you can actually investigate. Luke's Gospel opens with its writer saying he carefully investigated everything from the beginning, “so that you may know the certainty of the things you have been taught” (Luke 1:4). Read it. Ask your hardest questions out loud. We adults should have made this room safe for them a long time ago. The faith you were handed can become your own, and the Jesus who came back for Thomas isn't afraid of your questions.

scriptureStudy.note: A father whose son has suffered since childhood brings him to Jesus after the disciples fail to help. His prayer holds belief and unbelief together, and Jesus answers it by healing the boy and lifting him by the hand. Honest, mixed faith is still faith that Jesus hears.

Thomas misses Jesus' first appearance to the disciples and won't believe on their word. Jesus returns, speaks peace, and invites Thomas to touch his wounds. His words “Stop doubting and believe” come with evidence attached, and Thomas answers, “My Lord and my God!” Then Jesus blesses “those who have not seen and yet have believed” (20:29), which takes in every student in the room.
Faith passes through people, from grandmother to mother to son, and yet it becomes Timothy's own. The letter calls it “sincere faith,” which means neither borrowed nor performed.

Timothy is told to continue in what he learned, partly because he knows the people he learned it from, and because the Scriptures he has known since infancy lead to salvation “through faith in Christ Jesus.” An inherited faith can be a starting place that leads to Christ.

At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple, “listening to them and asking them questions.” Then he goes home with his parents and is obedient to them. Questions and honor belong together, and the young Jesus shows both.
When many disciples leave, Peter stays, not because he understands everything but because he knows Jesus has “the words of eternal life.”

sessions.goingDeeper: For the group that wants to think harder, set the research beside the Bible. Kara Powell and Chap Clark's Sticky Faith, drawn from the Fuller Youth Institute's research on students moving from high school into college, reports that doubt itself isn't what harms young people's faith so much as unexpressed doubt, the question kept silent because nobody seemed safe to ask. Os Guinness's God in the Dark, an updated version of his earlier In Two Minds, argues that doubt is a mind suspended between faith and unbelief, to be understood and answered rather than feared or celebrated. Both fit Jude's command: “have mercy on those who doubt” (Jude 1:22). For students who want a place to start on the hardest questions, Rebecca McLaughlin's 10 Questions Every Teen Should Ask (and Answer) about Christianity is written for them. Then there's a harder conversation that faithful Christians have without agreeing. Churches differ about how children belong to the church: some baptize the infants of believing parents and later invite them to confirm the faith as their own, and others baptize only those who profess faith for themselves. Both traditions want what this session wants, a faith that becomes personal trust in Christ. Christians also differ about whether a true believer can finally fall away. Those are questions for your pastor and your family, not for settling in a youth room. What all of them affirm is enough for tonight: Jesus came back for Thomas.
sessions.caseStudy: Suppose a senior who grew up in the church, helps lead worship, and has gone on every mission trip stays after youth group and tells a leader quietly, in the corner of the room while others are still around, that they aren't sure they believe any of it anymore and that their parents would be crushed to know. Talk through how a wise leader responds. What should the leader say first, and what would make things worse? What might be behind the question, and how could the leader find out without interrogating? How might the student eventually talk with their parents, and how could the leader help with that? What would it look like to keep the conversation going over weeks rather than trying to fix it in one night? And what might this student need from the church that a single conversation can't give?

memoryVerse.text: I do believe; help my unbelief!

leaderPrimer:
Leading teenagers through these questions is a privilege, and it carries more weight than most volunteer roles, so read this whole primer before the first session. Students will trust you with more than you expect. That trust is the point of the study, and it has to be protected.

Never meet with a student alone in private, in person or online. Talk with a student where others can see you even if they can't hear you: the corner of the youth room while others are still there, a table in the church lobby, a bench outside the building. Have two adults present at every session. Keep your messages with students transparent, and follow your church's safeguarding policy on texting, social media, rides, and supervision; if your church doesn't have one, ask your pastor before you begin. Never collect or read students' handouts or reflection pages. Those belong to them.

The discussion questions invite; they never require. Any student may pass on any question, every time, without explaining why, and you must never press a student to disclose something private, in the group or afterward. Most questions are written so students can answer about people their age in general rather than about themselves. If a student begins to share something in the group that sounds like danger, gently stop, thank them, and say you'd like to hear more right after the session. Then follow up that same day.

If you're worried about a student, ask them privately and directly whether they're thinking about suicide; asking won't put the idea in their head, and it tells them they can talk to you. If a student tells you they are thinking about suicide or about hurting themselves, take it seriously every time, even if they laugh it off. Stay with them, and don't leave them alone. Thank them for telling you, and tell them plainly that you are going to help them get help, which means you can't keep it secret. Call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, together with them, and if anyone is in immediate danger, call 911. Tell their parent or guardian, unless the parent or guardian is the danger, and tell your pastor or the person your church's policy names. Never treat it as a discipline problem or a failure of faith. Don't try to be their counselor; your job is to get them to people who can help and to stay close while that happens. Never discuss methods or details of self-harm in the group.

If a student tells you they are being hurt, threatened, or neglected, or that they don't feel safe at home, believe them and tell them they were right to tell you. Don't investigate, don't question them for details, and don't confront the person they named. Don't press the student to forgive or make peace with that person either; safety comes before reconciliation. Don't promise to keep it secret. Report it as the law requires and as your church's policy directs. Youth leaders are often mandated reporters, and the laws vary by state, so find out before the study begins what your state requires of you and whom your church notifies; nothing in this guide is legal advice. If a student is in immediate danger, call 911. For a student who is afraid of someone at home, the National Domestic Violence Hotline (call 1-800-799-7233 or text START to 88788) can also help, at any hour.

Know your room. Some students come from strong Christian homes, some from homes where faith isn't shared, and some from homes that are hard. Some are growing up without a father at home, and they may hear the word Father differently when the study uses it for God; Psalm 68 calls God “A father of the fatherless” (Psalm 68:5), and you can say so gently. Some students may not believe at all; welcome them without making them a project. Some are carrying anxiety or sadness that is more than a hard week. The third session says plainly that seeing a doctor or counselor is not a failure of faith, and you should say it too; nothing in this study is medical advice. For your own preparation, the site's pages on worry (/help/anxiety), loneliness (/help/loneliness), and doubt (/help/doubt) go further than a study guide can.

Questions about sexuality and gender may come up, in general or about a student's own life. This study doesn't take them up, and you shouldn't take a side on them in the room. If a student raises one, thank them, don't let it turn into a debate or let anyone mock the question, and offer to talk privately afterward, where others can see you. Then connect the student with your pastor and, where it's safe for the student, help them talk with their parents. What a student tells you about their own life is theirs; don't pass it on except as their safety requires and your pastor advises.

Some questions in this study are open among faithful Christians, and the study leaves them open. Families decide differently when a student should have a smartphone or social media, and no student should be shamed for what their family decided. Churches differ about how children belong to the church, whether through infant baptism and later confirmation or through believer's baptism, and about whether a true believer can finally fall away. Christians differ about which kinds of counseling are wisest and about when medication is the right help, though the study holds the floor that getting help is not a lack of faith. James Bell's own landing on these questions is not given here; that is his to say in his own words. Your job is to let students and families disagree and remain brothers and sisters.

Finally, lead from inside. The adults in the room aren't outside these questions. Adults perform for approval, scroll past midnight, worry about the future, get lonely, and borrow their convictions too. Where that's true of you, say so; students can tell the difference between an adult who is lecturing and one who is learning alongside them. Keep parents close: invite them to the orientation, tell them what each session covers, and remind them that they can read every handout. You won't fix anyone in five sessions, and you aren't supposed to. You're there to tell students the truth about who they are, to be safe and trustworthy, and to point them, yourself first, to the God who has spoken first.

faq.q: Is this study appropriate for my teenager? What does it cover, and what doesn't it?
faq.a: It is written for students roughly thirteen to eighteen, and parents can read every word their students read. The five sessions cover identity, the phone, anxiety, friendship and belonging, and doubt and owning faith. The study does not take up dating, sexuality, or gender, and it never asks students to share private information. When it touches heavy subjects, like anxiety or a friend in danger, it does so carefully: it tells students to talk to a trusted adult, it never describes self-harm, and it gives leaders clear instructions for keeping students safe.

faq.q: Will students be asked to share personal things in front of the group?
faq.a: No. Every discussion question invites and none require. Students may pass on any question at any time, and most questions are written so students can answer about people their age in general rather than about themselves. The leader primer tells leaders never to press a student to disclose anything private and never to collect or read students' reflection pages. If a student starts to share something that sounds like danger, the leader gently stops and talks with the student privately afterward, somewhere other people can see them.

faq.q: Does the study tell students to get rid of their phones or quit social media?
faq.a: No. The second session starts with the real goods of the phone and only then names the costs. It presents the strongest arguments on both sides, including Jonathan Haidt's case for delaying smartphones and social media and the criticism that the evidence is weaker than he claims. Whether and when a student has a phone or social media is a decision for each family, and faithful Christian parents decide it differently. The study's question is deeper than a rule: what are we becoming by what we keep looking at?

faq.q: My teenager struggles with anxiety. Will this study make them feel it's a lack of faith?
faq.a: It works hard to do the opposite. The third session says plainly that being anxious is not proof of weak faith, pointing to Jesus, who was deeply troubled and distressed in Gethsemane. It treats anxiety as something that can involve both body and soul, says that seeing a doctor or counselor is not a failure of faith, and tells students when to talk to a trusted adult and get help. It also teaches simple practices of prayer from Philippians 4 and 1 Peter 5. Nothing in the study is medical advice; if you're concerned, talk with your student's doctor.

faq.q: What happens if a student tells a leader they're thinking about suicide or hurting themselves?
faq.a: The leader primer tells leaders who are worried about a student to ask privately and directly, and if a student says yes, to take it seriously every time, stay with the student, tell them they're going to help them get help and so can't keep it secret, and call or text 988, the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, together. If anyone is in immediate danger, the leader calls 911. The leader tells the student's parent or guardian, unless the parent or guardian is the danger, and follows the church's safeguarding policy. Students are also told directly, in the first, third, and fourth sessions, that telling an adult is brave and that they can call or text 988 any time.

faq.q: What happens if a student tells a leader something is wrong at home?
faq.a: Leaders are instructed to believe the student, to tell them they were right to tell, and not to investigate, question them for details, or confront anyone. They don't promise secrecy. They report as the law requires and as the church's policy directs. Many youth leaders are mandated reporters, and the laws vary by state, so the primer tells every leader to learn their own obligations before the study begins; nothing in this guide is legal advice. The fourth session also teaches students that if a friend says they aren't safe, the loving thing is to tell a trusted adult, and that a student who isn't safe at home should tell a trusted adult outside the home, such as a teacher, a school counselor, or a pastor.

faq.q: Does this study encourage students to question their parents' faith?
faq.a: It encourages students to bring their real questions to Jesus, which is different. The fifth session takes seriously that a faith only borrowed to keep the peace isn't the same as trusting Christ yourself, and it takes just as seriously that a faith handed down is a gift. It points to Timothy, whose faith first lived in his grandmother and mother and became his own, and to the boy Jesus asking questions in the temple and then going home and obeying his parents. Owning faith, it says, means examining what you were given and choosing to trust Christ, not throwing everything away.

faq.q: My student has told me they have doubts. Should I be worried?
faq.a: Take it seriously, but don't panic. Doubt isn't the same as unbelief; it's being in two minds, and Scripture is full of people who brought their questions to God, from the psalmists to Thomas. The Fuller Youth Institute's research, described in Sticky Faith, found that doubt itself isn't what tends to harm young people's faith; doubt kept silent is. So the most helpful thing a parent can do is make it safe to keep talking: ask what's behind the question, listen more than you answer, and look for good answers together.

faq.q: Can a student come if they're not a Christian?
faq.a: Yes, and they're welcome. The study doesn't assume everyone in the room believes, and it never asks anyone to pretend. Students who don't believe will find hard questions taken seriously, objections stated fairly, and Christian claims put plainly enough to test. The fifth session says that whether Jesus rose from the dead is a question a person can actually investigate. Leaders are asked to welcome such students without making them a project.

faq.q: If I have doubts, does that mean I was never really a Christian?
faq.a: No. Christians from different traditions answer some related questions differently, such as whether a true believer can finally fall away, and the study leaves those for you to talk through with your pastor and family. But they agree that having doubts doesn't prove a person was never a Christian. Doubt is not the same as unbelief, and Jesus doesn't throw doubters away. He came back for Thomas, and he answered the father who asked for help with his unbelief. Bring your questions to Jesus in prayer and to a trusted Christian adult, and keep going.

faq.q: Why does the study keep pointing at the adults?
faq.a: Because much of what teenagers struggle with didn't start with them. Adults handed young people phones before learning to use their own, built the pressure around achievement, modeled worry and busyness, and often passed on a faith thinner than the one in the Bible; Kenda Creasy Dean's Almost Christian argued that teenagers' faith largely mirrors the faith of the adults around them. A study that corrected only teenagers would be dishonest, so this one asks the adults to go first.

faq.q: I'm a volunteer, not a youth pastor. Can I lead this?
faq.a: Yes. The study is built so a volunteer doesn't have to write a lesson: every discussion question has the answer behind it, every session has a backup question for a quiet room, and every session ends in prayer. What you do need is to read the leader primer, know your church's safeguarding policy and your state's reporting obligations, have two adults present, never meet with a student alone in private, and be honest with students about your own questions. You don't have to have everything figured out. You do have to be safe, truthful, and kind.

timeline.event: Augustine writes his Confessions. The book opens with his prayer that our hearts are restless until they rest in God, and it later admits that in his sixteenth year he stole pears with a group of friends and would not have done it alone.

The Heidelberg Catechism is published, a book of questions and answers written to teach the faith to young people. Its first question asks what your only comfort is in life and in death, and its answer begins by saying that you are not your own but belong, body and soul, to your faithful Savior Jesus Christ.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer publishes Life Together, written out of the shared life of the Confessing Church seminary at Finkenwalde, which the Gestapo had closed in 1937. He calls Christian community a gift of grace and warns that a dream of community, loved more than the real one, destroys it.
C. S. Lewis publishes The Four Loves, drawn from radio talks he gave in 1958, picturing friends not face to face like lovers but side by side, absorbed in some common interest.

Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton publish Soul Searching, a national study of American teenagers' religious lives, and give the name moralistic therapeutic deism to the thin working creed they found.

Kenda Creasy Dean publishes Almost Christian, arguing that teenagers' lukewarm faith largely reflects the faith of the adults and churches around them, and that the most committed young Christians share a story of God, a faith community, a sense of vocation, and hope.

Kara Powell and Chap Clark publish Sticky Faith, drawn from the Fuller Youth Institute's research on students moving into college, which found that unexpressed doubt, more than doubt itself, harms young people's faith. Sherry Turkle publishes Alone Together the same year.
Andy Crouch publishes The Tech-Wise Family and Tony Reinke publishes 12 Ways Your Phone Is Changing You, two Christian attempts to name both the gifts and the costs of the smartphone.

Kara Powell and Brad Griffin publish 3 Big Questions That Change Every Teenager, naming identity, belonging, and purpose as the questions underneath adolescence, and Alan Noble publishes You Are Not Your Own, building on the Heidelberg Catechism's first answer.

Jonathan Haidt publishes The Anxious Generation, arguing that the shift from a play-based to a phone-based childhood has harmed young people's mental health, a claim many parents find persuasive and some researchers contest.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome. I'm glad you're here. Before we start, here's how this group works. First, you never have to share anything you don't want to. Every question is an invitation, and you can always say pass, no explanation needed. Second, what people share here stays here, with one exception: if someone tells us they're being hurt, or that they might hurt themselves or someone else, we will get help, because keeping you safe matters more than keeping a secret. Third, questions are welcome, the hard ones and the doubting ones too. If you're not sure you believe any of this, you're welcome here, and nobody wants you to pretend. Fourth, the adults in this room don't have all of this figured out. Adults wrestle with a lot of the same things you do, and we're here to learn with you, not to lecture you. Tonight we're looking at this together: ________. Let's read our key passage, and then we'll talk.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked at what the passage says. Now let's bring it into the week you're actually going to have, the hallway, the group chat, the practice field, the kitchen table, the phone on your nightstand, because that's where this either matters or it doesn't.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though there's more to say. Try the practice this week if you can, and if you only manage the reflection questions, that counts. Your handout is yours, and nobody is going to collect it. If anything tonight stirred up something heavy, talk to me or another leader before you leave, or to a parent or another adult you trust tonight. And if you or a friend are ever in danger or thinking about hurting yourselves, tell a trusted adult right away, or call or text 988, any time. Let's pray before we go. Thanks for being honest tonight.

cadences.name: The full study (8 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Invite parents for the first twenty minutes to hear the plan, the ground rules, and how the group keeps students safe. Then set the ground rules with students and open session 1's first two questions slowly.
Week 2: Session 1, Who Says Who I Am?, full discussion and practice.
Week 3: Session 2, The Phone in My Pocket, part one: the honest gifts, the honest costs, and what comparison does to us.
Week 4: Session 2 continued: what we behold shapes us, with time to try the practice together and talk about how it went.
Week 5: Session 3, When I'm Anxious, with unhurried time on when to tell a trusted adult and how to get help.
Week 6: Session 4, Friends, Loneliness, and Belonging, including the scenario about a friend in danger.
Week 7: Session 5, A Faith That's Actually Mine.
Week 8: Integration. Revisit the memory verses and practices, and invite parents, grandparents, or older church members to share a meal with the group and hear whatever students choose to say.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, who says who I am and the phone in my pocket.
Week 2: Session 3, When I'm Anxious, with extra time on getting help.
Week 3: Session 4, Friends, Loneliness, and Belonging.
Week 4: Session 5, A Faith That's Actually Mine, plus a short close that returns to the word the Father spoke over Jesus at his baptism: beloved.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, Who Says Who I Am?
Week 2: Session 2, The Phone in My Pocket.
Week 4: Session 4, Friends, Loneliness, and Belonging.
Week 5: Session 5, A Faith That's Actually Mine.

bibliography.title: You Are Not Your Own: Belonging to God in an Inhuman World
bibliography.author: Alan Noble
bibliography.note: Builds on the first question of the Heidelberg Catechism to argue that the modern assumption that we belong to ourselves leaves each person responsible for making and justifying their own life, and that belonging to Christ is the better news. Behind session 1.

bibliography.title: When People Are Big and God Is Small: Overcoming Peer Pressure, Codependency, and the Fear of Man
bibliography.author: Edward T. Welch
bibliography.note: Names the fear of man, letting other people's approval and rejection rule us, which in teenagers is called peer pressure, and argues that the fear of the Lord frees us to need people less and love them more. Session 1.

bibliography.title: The Freedom of Self-Forgetfulness: The Path to True Christian Joy
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: A short exposition of 1 Corinthians 3:21-4:7 arguing that gospel humility frees a person from both pride and self-condemnation, because the Lord's judgment, not the crowd's or our own, is the one that counts. Session 1.

bibliography.title: Faith for Exiles: 5 Ways for a New Generation to Follow Jesus in Digital Babylon
bibliography.author: David Kinnaman and Mark Matlock
bibliography.note: Drawn from research on young Christians whose faith stayed resilient, it describes today's screen-saturated culture as digital Babylon and names five practices, beginning with intimacy with Jesus as the ground of a resilient identity. Sessions 1 and 2.

bibliography.title: The Tech-Wise Family: Everyday Steps for Putting Technology in Its Proper Place
bibliography.author: Andy Crouch
bibliography.note: Ten household commitments, such as waking up before our devices do and putting them to bed before we sleep, built on the conviction that choices about technology are really about forming wisdom and courage together. Session 2, and a gift to parents.

bibliography.title: 12 Ways Your Phone Is Changing You
bibliography.author: Tony Reinke
bibliography.note: A Christian account of how smartphones change us for good and for ill, from real gifts of connection to distraction, loneliness, and approval-seeking, written to help readers keep the gifts and avoid the pitfalls. Session 2.

bibliography.title: We Become What We Worship: A Biblical Theology of Idolatry
bibliography.author: G. K. Beale
bibliography.note: Traces through the whole canon, with Isaiah 6 as a lens, the principle that people come to resemble what they revere, for ruin or for restoration. The scholarly background to session 2's reading of Psalm 115 and 2 Corinthians 3:18, written for serious readers.

bibliography.title: Alone Together: Why We Expect More from Technology and Less from Each Other
bibliography.author: Sherry Turkle
bibliography.note: An MIT researcher's study of how constant connection changes relationships, arguing that we have come to expect more from our devices and less from one another. Not a Christian book; useful in sessions 2 and 4.

bibliography.title: The Anxious Generation
bibliography.author: Jonathan Haidt
bibliography.note: A social psychologist's argument that the shift from a play-based to a phone-based childhood harmed young people through social deprivation, sleep deprivation, fragmented attention, and addiction, with four proposed norms for families and schools. Some researchers dispute how much the evidence shows. Not a Christian book; sessions 2 and 3.

bibliography.title: Soul Searching: The Religious and Spiritual Lives of American Teenagers
bibliography.author: Christian Smith with Melinda Lundquist Denton
bibliography.note: The national study of American teenagers' religious lives that named moralistic therapeutic deism, a working creed in which God exists, wants people to be good and nice, helps when called on, and the goal of life is to be happy and feel good about oneself. Session 5.

bibliography.title: Almost Christian: What the Faith of Our Teenagers Is Telling the American Church
bibliography.author: Kenda Creasy Dean
bibliography.note: Argues from the same national study that teenagers' thin faith largely mirrors the faith of the adults and churches around them, and that the most committed young Christians share a personal story of God, a significant faith community, a sense of vocation, and hope. Sessions 4 and 5.

bibliography.title: Sticky Faith: Everyday Ideas to Build Lasting Faith in Your Kids
bibliography.author: Kara E. Powell and Chap Clark
bibliography.note: Draws on the Fuller Youth Institute's research on students moving from high school into college, including the finding that doubt itself is not what harms young people's faith; unexpressed doubt is. Session 5, and a gift to parents.

bibliography.title: 3 Big Questions That Change Every Teenager: Making the Most of Your Conversations and Connections
bibliography.author: Kara Powell and Brad M. Griffin
bibliography.note: Organizes adolescence around three questions, who am I, where do I fit, and what difference can I make, and offers research-based help for adults who walk with teenagers through identity, belonging, and purpose. Sessions 1 and 4.

bibliography.title: God in the Dark: The Assurance of Faith Beyond a Shadow of Doubt
bibliography.author: Os Guinness
bibliography.note: An updated version of his earlier In Two Minds, arguing that doubt is not the same as unbelief but a mind in two minds, suspended between faith and unbelief, to be understood and answered rather than feared or celebrated. Session 5.

bibliography.title: Life Together
bibliography.author: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bibliography.note: Written out of the shared life of the Confessing Church seminary at Finkenwalde, it treats Christian community as a gift of grace and warns that a dream of community, loved more than the real community, destroys it. Session 4.

bibliography.title: The Four Loves
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Distinguishes affection, friendship, romantic love, and charity, and pictures friends not face to face like lovers but side by side, absorbed in some common interest. Session 4.

bibliography.title: Confessions
bibliography.author: Augustine of Hippo
bibliography.note: Includes his account of stealing pears in his sixteenth year with friends, which he admits he would not have done alone, and his prayer that our hearts are restless until they rest in God. Sessions 3 and 4.

bibliography.title: 10 Questions Every Teen Should Ask (and Answer) about Christianity
bibliography.author: Rebecca McLaughlin
bibliography.note: Written for teenagers and building on her Confronting Christianity, it takes the hard questions young people ask about Christianity seriously, including questions about sexuality and gender, so parents may want to read it alongside their student. Session 5.

furtherReading: 10 Questions Every Teen Should Ask (and Answer) about Christianity, Rebecca McLaughlin, for students who want honest answers to hard questions. It also takes up sexuality and gender, so parents may want to read along.
The Tech-Wise Family, Andy Crouch, for parents and students who want to make decisions about screens together, as a household, instead of in a running argument.

3 Big Questions That Change Every Teenager, Kara Powell and Brad M. Griffin, for parents, grandparents, and leaders who want better conversations with teenagers about identity, belonging, and purpose.
You Are Not Your Own, Alan Noble, for older students and adults who want to think hard about why the modern demand to make yourself is so exhausting.
God in the Dark, Os Guinness, for anyone carrying doubts who wants them taken seriously, neither feared nor celebrated.

glossary.definition: The truth from Genesis 1 that God made every human being in his own likeness, to know him and to represent him in the world. It is given, not earned, so no grade, ranking, or failure can add to a person's worth or take it away. Sin damages the image but does not erase it.
The word the Father spoke over Jesus at his baptism, before any public ministry. In Christ, believers are brought into that love, so God's love is their starting point rather than their reward.

Letting other people's approval or rejection rule us. Teenagers call it peer pressure and adults call it people-pleasing; Scripture's answer is the fear of the Lord, which frees us to need people less and love them more.
What we give our eyes and minds to. The study treats attention as a form of love and a gift from God, which is why what holds it matters so much.
The slow shaping of a person by what they repeatedly do, love, and look at. Scripture teaches that we become like what we worship, either for ruin or for restoration.

A heavy, often physical sense of dread or alarm, usually fastened onto a future that hasn't happened yet. It can be part of ordinary life, and it can also be part of a medical condition that needs a doctor's care. Being anxious is not, in itself, a sin or proof of weak faith.
The peace Paul promises in Philippians 4, which surpasses understanding and guards the heart and mind in Christ Jesus. Sometimes it's felt as calm, and sometimes as the strength to keep going.
The word the first letter of Peter uses for what to do with anxiety: throw it onto God, because he cares for you. It's an act, often repeated, not a feeling.
A binding promise of loyal love. Jonathan's covenant with David shows friendship as committed love that lasts through danger and refuses rivalry.
The Berean Standard Bible's rendering of the Hebrew word hesed, the steady covenant love of God, which Jonathan asks David to show to his family.
The ache of not being known or not being wanted, which can happen even among many people. Being alone is the first thing in the creation story that God calls not good (Genesis 2:18).
The church understood as a family that Jesus creates, where believers of every age are brothers and sisters, mothers and fathers to one another.

Being in two minds, caught between faith and unbelief. Unlike unbelief, which has decided against God, doubt is a question that can still be brought to him, and Scripture commands mercy for those who doubt.

The name the sociologists Christian Smith and Melinda Lundquist Denton gave to the thin working creed they found among many American teenagers: God exists, wants people to be good and nice, helps when needed, and the goal of life is to be happy and feel good about oneself.

A person whom the law requires to report suspected abuse or neglect of a child. Many youth leaders are mandated reporters, and the rules vary by state, so every leader should learn their own obligations.

A church's written practices for protecting children and teenagers, such as never meeting with a student alone in private and reporting concerns. Every leader of this study should know it and follow it.

quoteCards: You're not a project you have to finish. You're someone God has already named.
The voices that want to own you usually start with if. Jesus answered the tempter with what God had already said.
You become like what you keep looking at. The feed is asking for your eyes, and so is Jesus. Only one of them knows your name.
Being anxious isn't proof of weak faith. Jesus was deeply troubled in the garden, and he took it to his Father.
Telling a trusted adult isn't a failure of faith. It's one of the ways God takes care of you.
Saul kept a jealous eye on David. Jonathan gave him his robe. Sooner or later, most friendships come to that choice.

Jesus came back for Thomas. He isn't afraid of your questions.
